2022_276_2_a_2022_troy_k12_board_letter_.paragraph: Plante & Moran, PLLC's draft Report to the Board of Education presents the results of the firm's audit of Troy School District's basic financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2022, together with other recommendations and a long set of informational items on Michigan school funding, retirement system liabilities, and upcoming accounting standards. The letter, dated October 4, 2022 and signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager, reports no disagreements with management and no significant difficulties. It states that General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $247,000 during 2021-2022, leaving fund balance at approximately $33,000,000, equal to 19.12 percent of expenditures and about 9.9 weeks of operations, and it flags that the Food Service Fund balance exceeds the USDA's three-month maximum and will require a spend-down plan submitted to the Michigan Department of Education.
2022_276_2_a_2022_troy_k12_board_letter_.page:
**Document and authorship**
Draft "Report to the Board of Education," Troy School District, June 30, 2022, prepared by Plante & Moran, PLLC; signed by Donna Hanson, CPA (Partner) and Michael Walsh, CPA (Senior Manager); dated October 4, 2022. Sections: Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), Informational Items (pages 7-16). The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the business office.

**Results of the audit**
Engagement letter dated June 1, 2022; planning matters discussed at a meeting on July 29, 2022; audit performed under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards and Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States. A separate letter dated October 4, 2022 addresses internal control over financial reporting and compliance testing, and a report on federal programs under 2 CFR Part 200 is likewise dated October 4, 2022. The management representation letter is dated October 4, 2022. The School District adopted GASB Statement No. 87, Leases, as of July 1, 2021, as described in Note 2. The auditors report no transactions lacking authoritative guidance, no significant transactions recorded in a different period, no significant difficulties, no disagreements with management, no consultations with other accountants, and that management corrected all immaterial misstatements. The most sensitive estimates were the District's share of MPSERS net liabilities under GASB 68 and GASB 75, estimated at June 30, 2022 as $210,869,230 (pension) and $13,509,781 (OPEB), based on data from the Office of Retirement Services.

**Other recommendations and observations**
- GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1 clarifies that items purchased in a group that fall below the capitalization threshold individually but exceed it in aggregate belong in fixed asset records; effective for the year ending June 30, 2024.
- Food Service Fund balance exceeds the U.S. Department of Agriculture maximum of three months of operating expenditures; a spend-down plan must be submitted to the Michigan Department of Education.

**School funding highlights**

| Item | Figure |
| --- | --- |
| 2021/2022 target foundation allowance | $8,700 per pupil |
| Prior target level | $8,529 per pupil |
| Minimum 2021/2022 increase, all districts | $171 per pupil |
| Troy foundation allowance 2021/2022 | $9,430 per pupil, up $115 |
| 2022/2023 target foundation allowance | $9,150 per pupil, a $450 / 5.2 percent increase |
| MPSERS overall contribution rate 2022 | 43 percent, from 42 percent |
| MPSERS overall contribution rate 2023 | 45 percent, from 43 percent |
| District net MPSERS cost | approximately 28 percent |

State retirement support received by the District: $1,062,198 under Section 147a1, $1,841,462 under 147a2, $13,922,709 under 147c1, and $311,632 under 147e. Other state actions cited include $475 million for a school consolidation and infrastructure fund, 1,300 new GSRP openings, $10,000 in tuition support for future teachers, $9,600 per-semester stipends for student teachers, full funding of Section 31a At-Risk, and a 5.2 percent ISD operations increase. Pupil counts use the 90 percent fall / 10 percent spring blend.

**Fund balance**
General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $247,000 in 2021-2022, with fund balance at approximately $33,000,000 at June 30, 2022 - 19.12 percent of expenditures, about 9.9 weeks of operations. The statewide average at June 30, 2021 was approximately 19.30 percent, roughly 10.0 weeks.

**MPSERS plan status and future standards**
At September 30, 2021 the MPSERS net pension liability was approximately $24.2 billion (down about 30 percent from $35 billion) and net OPEB liability approximately $1.5 billion (down about 72 percent from $5.4 billion), driven by a 27.2 percent investment return. Coming changes: the GASB financial reporting model exposure draft (final standard targeted December 2023, adoption June 30, 2025 for districts over $75 million in revenue), GASB 96 on subscription-based IT arrangements (June 30, 2023), and GASB 101 on compensated absences (June 30, 2025). A cybersecurity section cites the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021.
2022_276_2_a_2022_troy_k12_board_letter_.verbose:
Plante & Moran, PLLC prepared this draft "Report to the Board of Education" for Troy School District covering the audit of the basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2022. The letter is dated October 4, 2022 and is signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager. It is organized into three parts: Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-16). The cover letter extends thanks to Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness during the audit.

**Results of the audit.** The auditors state their responsibility under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management under the Board's oversight are fairly presented in all material respects in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, obtaining reasonable but not absolute assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement. Internal control was considered solely to determine audit procedures, not to provide assurance on such control. The audit was also conducted under Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, and a separate letter dated October 4, 2022 was issued on the consideration of internal control over financial reporting and on tests of compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements. The engagement letter is dated June 1, 2022, and planning matters were communicated at a meeting on July 29, 2022; the audit was performed according to that planned scope and timing.

**Significant audit findings.** Significant accounting policies are described in Note 2; as described there, the School District adopted Governmental Accounting Standards Board Statement No. 87, Leases, as of July 1, 2021, as required by the standard. The auditors noted no transactions entered into during the year for which there is a lack of authoritative guidance or consensus, and no significant transactions recognized in a period different from when they occurred. The most sensitive estimates affecting the financial statements were the School District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for the pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75; the District's estimates as of June 30, 2022 were $210,869,230 for pension and $13,509,781 for OPEB, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. No significant difficulties were encountered, no disagreements with management arose, management corrected all immaterial misstatements identified, disclosures are described as neutral, consistent, and clear, and there were no consultations with other independent accountants. A management representation letter dated October 4, 2022 was obtained. An audit of federal programs required by 2 CFR Part 200 was completed, with the compliance report to the Board dated October 4, 2022. The auditors read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and nothing came to their attention suggesting the other information is materially misstated or inconsistent. The information is intended solely for the use of the Board of Education and management.

**Other recommendations and observations.** Two items are raised. First, GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1 clarifies that items purchased in a group that are individually below a district's capitalization threshold but exceed the threshold in the aggregate should be reported in fixed asset records; this clarified guidance takes effect commencing with the year ending June 30, 2024, and the District should review its practices and written policies. Second, the fund balance of the Food Service Fund exceeds the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures, and the District will be required to develop a spend-down plan and submit it to the Michigan Department of Education.

**Informational items - school funding.** The report describes movement from projected pandemic hardships to the largest level of funding since the start of Proposal A (1994/1995). Highlights include elimination of the gap between base and target foundation levels in 2021/2022, the largest per-pupil funding increase since Proposal A in 2022/2023, increased state contributions above constitutional minimums for special education, increased contributions to reduce long-term retirement system cost, state and federal resources for learning support, federal contributions toward pandemic staffing costs, one-time investments in education resources and technology, and federal investments to address learning loss.

For 2021/2022, the School Aid Fund had a surplus for fiscal 2021 and the Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference predicted sustainable revenue. All schools moved to the target foundation allowance of $8,700 per pupil, eliminating the equity gap, and all schools including hold harmless districts received an increase of at least $171 per pupil from the former target of $8,529. Troy's foundation allowance per pupil was $9,430, an increase of $115 from the 2021 level. Funding progress was also made on School Finance Research Collaborative recommendations covering special education, At-Risk, wraparound services such as nurses and counselors, and Great Start Readiness (GSRP).

For 2022/2023, the target foundation allowance rose by $450 per pupil to $9,150, a 5.2 percent increase, with hold harmless districts also receiving the $450 increase. The traditional blended pupil count continues at 90 percent weighting for the October 2022 count and 10 percent for the February 2022 count. Other items: continued increases in special education cost reimbursement, with 2022 and 2023 the first years since Proposal A that special education allocations exceeded state constitutional minimums; increased GSRP funding creating 1,300 new student openings; full funding of Section 31a At-Risk programs after prior prorations; increased career and technical education funding; increased student mental health funding; teacher recruitment resources including $10,000 in tuition support for future teachers, $9,600 stipends per semester for student teachers, and "Grow Your Own" programs; expansion of before- and after-school programs; dedicated school safety funding for school resource officers, intervention systems, and a school safety commission; increased retirement system contributions; $475 million of state aid allocated to a school consolidation and infrastructure fund, the first such state allocation; and an ISD operations allocation increase of 5.2 percent to mirror the foundation increase.

**Federal resources.** Federal assistance has arrived in waves beginning in 2020 with most funding ending in 2024. ESSER III, made available during 2021/2022, comprises ESSER III formula and ESSER III equalization (Section 11t of PA 48 of 2021), is funded under the American Rescue Plan, and carries more restrictions than ESSER I and II; its funding period ends during 2024 and it is the last iteration of pandemic funding expected. In 2021/2022 the "super blend" was not used and the historic 90/10 blend applied. Summer school and learning assistance funding from ESSER II and state appropriations spanned the 2021 and 2022 fiscal years.

**MPSERS costs.** For 2022, the overall contribution rate increased to 43 percent from 42 percent, with the net cost to the District approximating 28 percent. State support flows through Sections 147a, 147c, and 147e; the District received $1,062,198 in 147a1, $1,841,462 in 147a2, $13,922,709 in 147c1, and $311,632 of 147e funding. For 2023, the overall rate rises to 45 percent from 43 percent with the District's net cost continuing at up to approximately 28 percent; by comparison, the total contribution rate when Proposal A was adopted was 11 percent. Beginning in 2021/2022 the State increased its share of special education costs by 3 percent of those costs, continuing into 2022/2023 with a reduction in the foundation allowance credited against required state support.

**Enrollment and outlook.** Statewide enrollment has historically been slightly under 1.5 million students, declining about 10,000 per year before the pandemic, then falling in excess of 50,000 during the pandemic; some recovery is expected but not to pre-pandemic levels. The May 2022 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference projected surpluses for 2023, 2024, and 2025; the next conference is set for January 2023. Inflation and a potential recession are cited as the key risks, and the window for using the majority of federal pandemic funds closes by September 30, 2024.

**Grants management and budgeting.** The report describes increased grants management workload and risk across superintendents and leadership, board members, the business office, staff, procurement, information technology, and facilities, arising from ESSER, GEER, and CRF programs alongside traditional Title I, Special Education, and Child Nutrition grants, and recommends continued assessment of compliance risks moving into fiscal 2023.

**Fund balance.** During the 2021-2022 school year the School District's General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $247,000, leaving General Fund fund balance at approximately $33,000,000 at June 30, 2022. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2021 was approximately 19.30 percent of expenditures and outgoing transfers, equal to about 10.0 weeks of average operating costs. The School District's fund balance percentage is 19.12 percent, equal to approximately 9.9 weeks of operation. Consumer Price Index growth and decisions on spending COVID-19 relief funds are named as pressures on 2022-2023 fund balance.

**MPSERS plan net liabilities.** The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2021 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $24.2 billion, a decrease of approximately 30 percent from $35 billion at September 30, 2020, driven largely by net investment gains; the plan's annual investment rate of return was 27.2 percent for the year ended September 30, 2021 compared with 5.0 percent for the year ended September 30, 2020. The retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB liability of approximately $1.5 billion at September 30, 2021, down from $5.4 billion at September 30, 2020, a decrease of approximately 72 percent, reflecting the 27.2 percent return versus 4.9 percent the prior year. Because markets declined after the valuation date, both net liabilities are expected to increase significantly next year.

**Future GASB standards.** The financial reporting model project began in August 2013, with an exposure draft titled "Financial Reporting Model Improvements" issued in June 2020 and a comment period ending February 2021; Plante & Moran submitted comments, and the GASB's goal is a final standard by December 2023. Proposed changes include expanded management's discussion and analysis, a budget-to-actual column showing variances between original and amended budgets, terminology changes ("revenue" to "inflows of resources," "expenditures" to "outflows of resources"), and replacement of modified accrual with a "short-term financial resources measurement focus" recognizing transactions expected to be converted to or paid in cash within 12 months of year end, versus today's general 60-day receivable rule. Phased adoption would apply to districts with total annual revenue across all funds over $75 million in the year ending June 30, 2025, and to those under $75 million in the year ending June 30, 2026. A related project, the June 2020 preliminary views on "Revenue and Expense Recognition," could produce a standard during 2027. GASB Statement No. 96 on subscription-based information technology arrangements is effective for the District's June 30, 2023 financial statements and mirrors GASB 87, requiring a right-to-use subscription asset and subscription liability measured at net present value for arrangements generally exceeding one year, with fund-level expenditures reclassified as debt service payments. GASB Statement No. 101 on compensated absences, effective for the year ending June 30, 2025, requires a full accrual liability for leave attributable to services already rendered that accumulates and is more likely than not to be used or paid, measured at each employee's pay rate at the statement date, while removing gross addition and reduction disclosure and the requirement to disclose liquidating funds.

**Cybersecurity.** Education remains a top target for ransomware; the "K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021" was signed into law in October 2021. The letter notes that the human element is the weakest link, citing easily guessed passwords such as "August2022," raises questions about phishing awareness, data location, personally identifiable information and FERPA data on file-sharing sites or flash drives, and remote access security, and offers an external vulnerability assessment.

2022_278_8_a_2022_troy_board_presentatio.paragraph: Troy School District's draft audit presentation to the Board of Education covers the year ended June 30, 2022 and reports an unmodified opinion on the financial statements and an unmodified opinion on the federal program audit with no findings or questioned costs. It walks through non-recurring COVID-19 relief awards, governmental fund results, General Fund revenue and expenditure composition, per-pupil membership and foundation allowance history, and a ten-year fund balance trend. General Fund revenue of $170,116,893 against expenditures of $172,507,660, offset by net other financing sources of $2,637,502, produced a current-year increase of $246,735 and an ending fund balance of $32,980,837, equal to 19.12 percent of total expenditures and other uses, or 9.9 weeks and 70 days of operations.

2022_278_8_a_2022_troy_board_presentatio.verbose:
Draft board presentation for Troy School District covering the year ended June 30, 2022, delivered to the Board of Education as part of the annual audit report-out.

**Key 2022 audit highlights.** The presentation opens with the audit results: the 2022 financial statement audit produced an unmodified opinion, and the 2022 federal program audit produced an unmodified opinion with no findings or questioned costs. Additional topics listed are bond and sinking fund compliance, GASB 87 implementation, the Uniform Budget Act, the ASBO Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for 2021, non-recurring funding sources of revenue, federal ESSER, and federal child care grants.

**Non-recurring COVID-19 relief funding.** Awards and expenditures as of June 30, 2022 are presented in thousands, with total allocated of $27,757 and total expended of $19,028. By program, allocated and expended-to-date amounts are: CRF $6,501 allocated and $6,501 expended; ESSER I $246 and $246; ESSER II $1,074 allocated and $970 expended; ESSER II Equalization (State) $5,036 and $5,036; ESSER III $1,895 and $1,895; ESSER III Equalization - 11t $12,385 allocated and $3,760 expended; GEER $22 and $22; and ARP - IDEA $598 and $598. The ESSER III Equalization (Section 11t) line is the one with a large unspent balance remaining.

**Governmental funds revenue and expenditures.** Results are shown for three columns: the General Fund, the 2019 Capital Projects Fund, and Total Nonmajor Funds. Revenue was $170,116,893 in the General Fund, $23,498 in the 2019 Capital Projects Fund, and $40,854,075 in nonmajor funds. Expenditures were 172,507,660, 11,414,598, and 36,192,820 respectively, producing excess of revenue (under) over expenditures of (2,390,767), (11,391,100), and 4,661,255. Other financing sources and uses include transfers in of 1,200,000 in the General Fund and 8,411 in nonmajor funds; transfers out of (1,208,411) in nonmajor funds; leases entered into of 492,818 in nonmajor funds; and proceeds from sale of capital assets of 1,437,502 in the General Fund.
